title: I want to go to the island
title_target: Θέλω να πάω — Theh-loh nah pah-oh
goal: Say what you want, can, and must do — and face the fact that Greek has no basic verb form at all, nothing like "to go" or "to eat".
bekal: see that the second verb changes with its subject too
use μπορώ να, πρέπει να, ξέρω να
recognize the one-time form of the most common verbs
suggest with ας and negate with δεν

dialogs.title: ΔΙΑΛΟΓΟΣ — Island plans
dialogs.intro: Nikos and Ana make plans for the weekend. Count how many times **να** appears — nine times in eleven lines. That tiny word is the backbone of everyday Greek.

lines.speaker: Νίκος:
lines.id: What do you want to do this weekend?
lines.literal: what — you-want — that — you-do — the — weekend?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: I want to go to an island. Can I go by boat?
lines.literal: I-want — that — I-go — to — an — island. I-can — that — I-go — with — the — boat?

lines.speaker: Νίκος:
lines.id: Of course. But you have to buy a ticket early.
lines.literal: of-course. but — it-must — that — you-buy — ticket — early.

lines.speaker: Νίκος:
lines.literal: of-course! all — the — Greeks — they-know — that — they-swim.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: I want to learn to do it better, too.
lines.literal: I-want — that — I-learn — also — I — better.

lines.speaker: Νίκος:
lines.id: We can go together. We have to leave at seven.
lines.literal: we-can — that — we-go — together. it-must — that — we-leave — at — seven.

lines.speaker: Νίκος:
lines.id: The boat doesn't wait! Do you want to come?
lines.literal: the — boat — not — it-waits! you-want — that — you-come?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Yes, I do! What should I bring?
lines.literal: yes, I-want! what — it-must — that — I-take?

lines.speaker: Νίκος:
lines.id: A hat, water, and a good mood. Let's go!
lines.literal: hat, water, and — good — mood. let — we-go!

notes: ⚠️ **Greek has no basic verb form at all.** There is no single word meaning just "to go", like *to go* in English. Every verb is always tied to its subject. So "I want to go" needs **two** verbs, both saying "I": *θέλ**ω** να πά**ω***.

**That means both verbs change together.** Θέλω να π**άω** (I want to go) · Θέλεις να π**α**ς (you want to go) · Θέλει να π**άει** (he/she wants to go) · Θέλουμε να π**άμε** (we want to go). ⚠️ *Θέλω να πας* isn't wrong — it means "I want **you** to go". A subtle but very useful difference.

**Να itself has no translatable meaning.** The closest is "that" or "to", but in practice it's just the required link between two verbs. Think of it as a connector: whenever two verbs come in a row, να stands between them.

**Πρέπει never changes.** It means "must" and is always in the "it" form, whoever the subject: *Πρέπει να πάω* (I must go), *Πρέπει να πας* (you must go), *Πρέπει να φύγουμε* (we must leave). The subject is shown by the verb **after** να.

**The verb after να often uses a different form from its everyday one.** πηγαίνω → να **πάω**; τρώω → να **φάω**; πίνω → να **πιω**; βλέπω → να **δω**; έρχομαι → να **έρθω**; παίρνω → να **πάρω**; αγοράζω → να **αγοράσω**; μαθαίνω → να **μάθω**. ⚠️ This is called the **one-time form**, and it marks an action seen as one complete event, not a habit. It comes back for the future (unit 16) and the past (units 14–15), so every form you learn now gets used three times.

**If the action is repeated or ongoing, να takes the ordinary form**: *Θέλω να **πηγαίνω** στη θάλασσα κάθε μέρα* — I want to go to the sea every day. Compare *Θέλω να **πάω** στη θάλασσα* — I want to go to the sea (once, now).

**Negating: δεν before the first verb.** *Δεν θέλω να πάω.* — I don't want to go. If what you negate is the action itself, να takes **μην**: *Θέλω να **μην** πάω* — I'd like not to go. The first is far more common.
**Ας (*ahs*) + the "we" form = let's.** *Ας πάμε!* (let's go), *Ας φάμε!* (let's eat), *Ας δούμε* (let's see). It's a close cousin of να and, like it, has no single translation.

grammars.title: Four verbs always followed by να
body: These four cover nearly every A1 need for saying what you want, can, must, and know how to do.

head: First word
Meaning
Example
English
rows: I want to go to Crete.

after: ⚠️ **Μπορώ and ξέρω can both mean "can", but they differ.** *Μπορώ να κολυμπήσω* = circumstances let me swim right now. *Ξέρω να κολυμπάω* = I have the skill of swimming. English uses one word for both, so choose consciously.
For polite requests, **μπορώ να** is the safest form: *Μπορώ να έχω τον λογαριασμό;* — Can I have the bill?

grammars.title: The one-time form of the most common verbs
body: Bookmark this table. All fifteen forms below come back in units 14, 15, and 16 — learn them now and you pay once for three units.
after: The endings are exactly those of group A: **-ω, -εις, -ει, -ουμε, -ετε, -ουν**. So να πάω, να πας, να πάει, να πάμε, να πάτε, να πάνε. ⚠️ Πάω strays a little because its stem is short; the rest are perfectly regular.
**Είμαι and έχω have no one-time form** — after να they stay είμαι and έχω: *Θέλω να είμαι εκεί.* *Πρέπει να έχεις εισιτήριο.* The two most important verbs are the easiest ones here.

blocks.title: να sentences you'll use every day
items: **Μπορώ να έχω …;** — Can I have …? The politest request form, usable anywhere.
**Τι θέλεις να κάνεις;** — What do you want to do? · **Τι πρέπει να κάνω;** — What should I do?
**Θέλω να πάω στο …** — I want to go to … The lifesaver sentence in a taxi.
**Πρέπει να φύγω.** — I have to go. The politest way to end a conversation that has run long.
**Ας πάμε για καφέ.** — Let's get coffee. ⚠️ In Greece this isn't small talk: an invitation for coffee is almost always meant, and turning it down without a reason sounds cold.
**Δεν μπορώ σήμερα, αλλά ας πάμε αύριο.** — I can't today, but let's go tomorrow. The no-offense way to decline: say no, then offer an alternative.

exercises.prompt: Make the second verb match its subject.
items: Πρέπει να ____ εισιτήριο. (αγοράσω) — the subject is "you"

exercises.prompt: Change to the form used after να. Example: τρώω → να φάω.
Put the words in the right order.
Translate into Greek. Remember: two verbs, two endings.
items: I want to go to the beach.
We have to leave at seven.
